questions.title: How do you ensure compliance in AWS?
questions.answer: Compliance is ensured by using **AWS Artifact** for reports, **AWS Config** for resource auditing, **CloudTrail** for activity logs, and using 'compliant' regions or services that meet specific standards like HIPAA or PCI DSS.

questions.title: What is AWS Config?
questions.answer: AWS Config is a service that enables you to assess, audit, and evaluate the configurations of your AWS resources. It provides a detailed view of the configuration history and allows for automated compliance checking against 'Config Rules'.

questions.title: Describe the AWS Well-Architected Framework.
questions.answer: The Well-Architected Framework consists of six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, and Sustainability. It provides a consistent set of best practices to evaluate architectures.

questions.title: What is the AWS Well-Architected Framework?
questions.answer: It is a set of whitepapers and tools (Well-Architected Tool) designed to help cloud architects build the most secure, high-performing, resilient, and efficient infrastructure possible for their applications.

questions.title: How would you design a multi-tier application architecture in AWS?
questions.answer: A typical 3-tier architecture: 1. Presentation Tier (S3/CloudFront or ALB), 2. Application Tier (EC2 Auto Scaling in Private Subnets), 3. Data Tier (RDS Multi-AZ). Tiers are separated by subnets and Security Groups for isolation.

questions.title: Explain the concept of microservices and how AWS supports them.
questions.answer: Microservices break an application into small, independent services. AWS supports them via ECS/EKS (containers), Lambda (serverless), and API Gateway (entry point), using SQS/SNS for asynchronous communication between them.

questions.title: How can you implement a multi-account architecture in AWS?
questions.answer: Multi-account architecture is implemented using **AWS Organizations**. This allows for consolidated billing and logical separation of environments (Dev, Test, Prod) to minimize 'blast radius' and improve security boundaries.

questions.title: What is the purpose of AWS Organizations?
questions.answer: The purpose is to centralize management, simplify billing, and enforce policies (Service Control Policies or SCPs) across multiple AWS accounts from a single master account.

questions.title: How do you implement service discovery in AWS?
questions.answer: Service discovery is implemented using **AWS Cloud Map**. It allows services to discover each other via custom names. It integrates with ECS and EKS to automatically register and deregister service instances as they scale.

questions.title: Explain how you would architect a global application in AWS.
questions.answer: A global application uses: 1. CloudFront for static content, 2. Global Accelerator for dynamic traffic, 3. Multi-Region active-active setup with Route 53, and 4. Global Databases like DynamoDB Global Tables or Aurora Global Database.

questions.title: What are the considerations for using serverless architectures?
questions.answer: Considerations include: 1. Cold start latency, 2. Execution time limits, 3. Vendor lock-in, 4. Scalability benefits, and 5. Cost model (per request vs per hour). Serverless is ideal for event-driven, intermittent, or highly variable workloads.

questions.title: How do you manage serverless applications in AWS?
questions.answer: Serverless apps are managed using the **AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model)** or the **Serverless Framework**. These tools provide CLI and templates to define Lambda, API Gateway, and DynamoDB resources as a single unit.

questions.title: What are the key performance indicators for AWS services?
questions.answer: KPIs include: 1. Request Latency, 2. Error Rate (HTTP 5xx), 3. CPU/Memory Utilization, 4. Disk Throughput/IOPS, and 5. Throttling events in services like Lambda or DynamoDB.

questions.title: How do you evaluate and improve the architecture of an AWS solution?
questions.answer: Evaluation is done via the **AWS Well-Architected Tool**. Improvement involves identifying 'high-risk' findings and applying best practices like migrating to managed services, implementing Auto Scaling, or moving to a serverless model.

questions.title: What is AWS Systems Manager?
questions.answer: Systems Manager (SSM) is a management service that helps you automatically collect software inventory, apply OS patches, create system images, and configure Windows and Linux operating systems on EC2 and on-premises.

questions.title: How does AWS Batch work?
questions.answer: AWS Batch enables developers, scientists, and engineers to easily and efficiently run hundreds of thousands of batch computing jobs on AWS. It automatically provisions the optimal quantity and type of compute resources based on the specific requirements of the jobs.

questions.title: Explain how AWS App Mesh works.
questions.answer: AWS App Mesh is a service mesh that provides application-level networking. It gives you consistent visibility and network traffic controls for every microservice in an application, using the Envoy proxy to manage all communications.

questions.title: What is AWS Control Tower?
questions.answer: AWS Control Tower provides the easiest way to set up and govern a new, secure, multi-account AWS environment based on best practices. It automates the creation of a 'landing zone' with guardrails for governance and security.

questions.title: What is AWS Service Catalog?
questions.answer: AWS Service Catalog allows organizations to create and manage catalogs of IT services that are approved for use on AWS. This helps achieve consistent governance and meet compliance requirements while enabling users to quickly deploy only the approved services they need.

questions.title: How do you troubleshoot performance issues in AWS?
questions.answer: Troubleshooting involves: 1. Analyzing CloudWatch metrics and logs, 2. Tracing requests with AWS X-Ray, 3. Checking Trusted Advisor for performance findings, 4. Using VPC Flow Logs to identify network latency, and 5. Reviewing EC2 'Status Checks'.

questions.title: What are the key considerations for choosing an instance type in EC2?
questions.answer: Considerations include the workload type (Compute vs Memory vs Storage intensive), the required network throughput, whether the load is consistent or burstable (T series), and the cost-performance balance of Graviton vs Intel/AMD processors.

docker-questions.title: Docker Questions
docker-questions.description: Comprehensive technical guide covering Docker Architecture, Images, Networking, Volumes, Orchestration (Swarm/K8s), and Security.

questions.title: What is Docker?
questions.answer: Docker is an open-source platform designed to automate the deployment, scaling, and management of applications using containerization. it allows developers to package an application with all its dependencies into a standardized unit called a container, ensuring it runs consistently across different computing environments.

questions.title: What are containers in Docker?
questions.answer: Containers are lightweight, standalone, and executable packages that include everything needed to run a piece of software, including the code, runtime, system tools, libraries, and settings. They isolate applications from each other and the underlying infrastructure.

questions.title: What is a Docker container?
questions.answer: A Docker container is a runtime instance of a Docker image. It is a sandboxed process on the host machine that is isolated from all other processes. Multiple containers can run on the same host, sharing the OS kernel but having their own file system and network stack.

questions.title: How is Docker different from virtual machines?
questions.answer: Virtual Machines (VMs) include a full guest operating system, making them heavy and slow to start. Docker containers share the host's OS kernel and isolate the application processes at the user level, making them much lighter, faster to boot, and more resource-efficient than VMs.

questions.title: What are the advantages of using Docker?
questions.answer: Advantages include: 1. Consistency across environments (Dev/Test/Prod). 2. Rapid deployment and scaling. 3. Resource efficiency through shared kernels. 4. Isolation and security. 5. Simplified dependency management and version control of infrastructure.

questions.title: What are the key components of Docker architecture?
questions.answer: The architecture follows a client-server model consisting of: 1. Docker Client (CLI tool). 2. Docker Host (running the Docker Daemon). 3. Docker Objects (Images, Containers, Networks, Volumes). 4. Docker Registry (Docker Hub or private registries).

questions.title: What is the role of the Docker daemon?
questions.answer: The Docker daemon (dockerd) is a persistent background process that manages Docker objects such as images, containers, networks, and volumes. It listens for Docker API requests and performs the heavy lifting of building and running containers.

questions.title: How does Docker handle container isolation?
questions.answer: Docker uses Linux kernel features to provide isolation. 'Namespaces' provide a private view of system resources (network, PID, mount), while 'Control Groups' (cgroups) limit and monitor resource usage like CPU and memory for each container.

questions.title: What are Docker namespaces and cgroups?
questions.answer: Namespaces are a kernel feature that isolates system resources per process (Network, User, UTS, Mount, IPC, PID). Cgroups (Control Groups) manage the resource allocation, ensuring a container doesn't consume all available CPU or RAM of the host.

questions.title: What is the purpose of a Docker image?
questions.answer: A Docker image serves as a read-only template used to create containers. It contains the application code, libraries, and environment configurations. Images are portable, allowing the same software to be deployed anywhere Docker is installed.

questions.title: What is the difference between a Docker container and a Docker image?
questions.answer: An image is a static, read-only blueprint (class), while a container is a dynamic, running instance (object) of that image. You can create multiple containers from a single image, and changes to a container do not affect the underlying image.

questions.title: How do you create a Docker image from a Dockerfile?
questions.answer: You use the 'docker build' command. This command reads the instructions in the Dockerfile and executes them step-by-step to produce a final image. Example: 'docker build -t my-app:v1 .'

questions.title: Explain the concept of image layers in Docker.
questions.answer: Docker images are composed of a series of read-only layers. Each instruction in a Dockerfile creates a new layer. These layers are cached and shared, making builds faster and reducing storage space. When a container runs, a thin 'writable layer' is added on top.

questions.title: What are Docker tags, and why are they important?
questions.answer: Tags are aliases for Image IDs, usually used for versioning (e.g., '1.0', 'latest', 'stable'). They are important because they allow developers to identify specific releases of an image and ensure the correct version is deployed in production.

questions.title: How can you optimize Docker images for production?
questions.answer: Optimization techniques include: 1. Using minimal base images (like Alpine). 2. Multi-stage builds to exclude build tools. 3. Minimizing the number of layers. 4. Using .dockerignore to exclude unnecessary files. 5. Leveraging layer caching efficiently.

questions.title: What is a Dockerfile?
questions.answer: A Dockerfile is a text document containing all the commands a user could call on the command line to assemble an image. Instructions like FROM, RUN, CMD, and ENTRYPOINT define the build process and the container's default behavior.

questions.title: What is Docker's COPY vs. ADD command?
questions.answer: COPY is preferred for simply moving local files into the container. ADD is more powerful as it can fetch files from URLs and automatically extract tar archives. Use COPY for transparency unless you specifically need the extra features of ADD.

questions.title: Explain the concept of a multi-stage Docker build.
questions.answer: Multi-stage builds allow you to use multiple 'FROM' statements in one Dockerfile. You can compile your code in a large 'build' stage and then copy only the resulting binary into a smaller 'production' stage, resulting in a significantly smaller and more secure image.

questions.title: What is the purpose of the .dockerignore file?
questions.answer: The .dockerignore file is used to exclude files and directories from the build context. This speeds up the build process and keeps the resulting image smaller by preventing unnecessary files (like .git, node_modules, or logs) from being sent to the Docker daemon.

questions.title: What is the difference between docker run and docker create?
questions.answer: 'docker create' initializes a container from an image and prepares it for running, but does not start it. 'docker run' is a combination of 'docker create' and 'docker start', creating and starting the container immediately.

questions.title: What is the difference between docker run and docker exec?
questions.answer: 'docker run' is used to create and start a NEW container. 'docker exec' is used to run a new command inside an ALREADY running container, which is useful for debugging or executing administrative tasks.

questions.title: What is the purpose of docker exec vs. docker attach?
questions.answer: 'docker exec' starts a new process inside the container, allowing you to leave it without stopping the container. 'docker attach' connects your terminal to the container's main process (PID 1); if you exit with Ctrl+C, the entire container usually stops.

questions.title: How do you run a container in detached mode?
questions.answer: You use the '-d' flag with the 'docker run' command. This runs the container in the background of your terminal, allowing you to continue using the terminal while the container executes. Example: 'docker run -d nginx'.

questions.title: How do you remove unused images, containers, and volumes in Docker?
questions.answer: You use the 'docker system prune' command. This safely removes stopped containers, unused networks, and dangling images. Adding the '-a' flag will also remove images not associated with any container, and '--volumes' will remove unused volumes.

questions.title: What is the lifecycle of a Docker container?
questions.answer: The lifecycle includes several states: 1. Created. 2. Running. 3. Paused. 4. Exited (Stopped). 5. Dead (Removal phase). Containers move between these states based on user commands or internal process completion.

questions.title: How do you configure automatic container restarts?
questions.answer: Using the '--restart' flag during 'docker run'. Options include 'no' (default), 'on-failure' (restart if process fails), 'always' (always restart), and 'unless-stopped' (restart unless manually stopped by the user).

questions.title: What is a Docker volume?
questions.answer: A Docker volume is a managed storage mechanism for persisting data generated and used by Docker containers. Volumes are stored on the host file system but managed by Docker, ensuring data survives even if the container is deleted.

questions.title: What are the differences between Docker volumes and bind mounts?
questions.answer: Volumes are managed by Docker and stored in a specific directory (/var/lib/docker/volumes). Bind mounts can be stored anywhere on the host system and rely on the host's directory structure, making them more dependent on the host's OS configuration.

questions.title: How does Docker networking work? Describe bridge, host, and overlay networks.
questions.answer: 1. Bridge: The default, creating a private network on the host. 2. Host: Shares the host's network stack directly (no isolation). 3. Overlay: Connects multiple Docker daemons across different hosts, enabling Swarm services to communicate securely.

questions.title: What is the use of Docker Compose?
questions.answer: Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container applications. Using a YAML file (docker-compose.yml), you can configure your application's services, networks, and volumes, and then start everything with a single command: 'docker-compose up'.

questions.title: What is Docker Swarm?
questions.answer: Docker Swarm is Docker's native orchestration tool. It allows you to manage a cluster of Docker nodes as a single virtual system, providing features like load balancing, service discovery, and rolling updates for containerized applications.

questions.title: What is the difference between a Docker container and a Docker service?
questions.answer: In a Swarm environment, a container is a single instance, while a service is the definition of the desired state (e.g., 'run 5 replicas of nginx'). The Swarm manager ensures that the specified number of containers (tasks) are running across the cluster.

questions.title: Explain the concept of container orchestration.
questions.answer: Orchestration is the automated management of container lifecycles in complex environments. It handles tasks like deployment, scaling, networking between containers, load balancing, and health monitoring (Self-healing).

questions.title: How do you secure Docker containers?
questions.answer: Security best practices include: 1. Running as non-root users. 2. Using trusted, scanned images. 3. Limiting container resources (cgroups). 4. Using read-only file systems. 5. Managing secrets securely using Swarm secrets or Vault. 6. Keeping the Docker daemon updated.

questions.title: What are the key differences between Docker and Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Docker is a platform for building and running containers on a single host. Kubernetes is a more complex orchestration platform designed to manage clusters of hosts running containers. Kubernetes offers more advanced self-healing, automated rollouts, and secret management than basic Docker.

questions.title: What is 'Docker in Docker' (DinD)?
questions.answer: DinD is the practice of running Docker inside a Docker container. It is commonly used in CI/CD pipelines to build and push Docker images. It requires the container to run in '--privileged' mode, which has significant security implications.

questions.title: How do you find the IP address of a running Docker container?
questions.answer: You can use the 'docker inspect' command along with a filter. Example: 'docker inspect -f "{{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}}{{end}}" container_id'.

questions.title: What is the purpose of the docker stats command?
questions.answer: The 'docker stats' command provides a live stream of resource usage statistics for running containers, including CPU percentage, memory usage, network I/O, and block I/O. It is essential for basic performance monitoring.

questions.title: How do you expose a Docker container's port to the host?
questions.answer: Using the '-p' or '--publish' flag. Example: 'docker run -p 8080:80 nginx' maps port 80 of the container to port 8080 of the host machine, making the service accessible externally.

questions.title: What is the difference between docker exec and docker attach?
questions.answer: 'exec' creates a new process (like a new shell), while 'attach' connects you to the existing process that started the container. If you exit 'attach', the container usually dies; if you exit 'exec', the container keeps running.

questions.title: Explain what a Docker container is.
questions.answer: A Docker container is a standardized, encapsulated environment that runs an application. It is isolated from the host OS and other containers using kernel namespaces and cgroups, providing a 'write once, run anywhere' experience.

questions.title: How are Docker containers different from virtual machines?
questions.answer: Containers are process-level isolation sharing one OS kernel. VMs are hardware-level isolation each with its own OS kernel. This makes containers faster to start (milliseconds vs minutes) and more portable.

questions.title: What is a Docker image?
questions.answer: A Docker image is a read-only, multi-layered file that includes the application code and all its dependencies. It is the persistent 'snapshot' from which containers are launched.

questions.title: What is the difference between an image and a container?
questions.answer: An image is the source code/blueprint; it is static. A container is the running process; it is dynamic. Think of an Image as a Program and a Container as a Process.

questions.title: What is the use of the docker build command?
questions.answer: It automates the creation of a Docker image by following instructions in a Dockerfile. It sends the 'build context' to the daemon and produces a tagged image in the local library.

questions.title: How do you pull a specific version of a Docker image?
questions.answer: By appending a colon and the tag name to the image name. Example: 'docker pull python:3.9-slim'. If no tag is specified, Docker defaults to ':latest'.

questions.title: How do you update a Docker image?
questions.answer: Images are immutable. To 'update' an image, you must modify the Dockerfile, run 'docker build' again to create a new version, and then restart your containers using the new image.

questions.title: How do you optimize Dockerfiles for faster builds and smaller images?
questions.answer: 1. Use .dockerignore. 2. Order instructions from least to most frequent change. 3. Combine RUN commands to reduce layers. 4. Use multi-stage builds. 5. Clear package manager caches (e.g., rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*).

questions.title: Explain the importance of using a base image with minimal attack surfaces.
questions.answer: Base images like 'Alpine' or 'Distroless' contain only the bare minimum files. This reduces the number of vulnerable binaries (like shells or package managers), making the container much harder for an attacker to exploit.

questions.title: What is Dockerfile and what is its purpose?
questions.answer: It is a script containing instructions to build a Docker image. Its purpose is to provide a version-controlled, repeatable way to document and automate the environment setup for an application.

questions.title: What are Dockerfile build arguments and how are they used?
questions.answer: Build arguments (ARG) allow you to pass variables into the Dockerfile during the build process ('--build-arg'). They are useful for setting version numbers or environment settings that shouldn't be hardcoded.

questions.title: How do you run a Docker container?
questions.answer: Using 'docker run [OPTIONS] IMAGE [COMMAND]'. Common options include '-d' (detached), '-p' (ports), and '--name' (custom name).

questions.title: How do you create a Docker container?
questions.answer: You can use 'docker create' to instantiate it without starting, or 'docker run' to both create and start it immediately.

questions.title: What command is used to enter inside a running container?
questions.answer: 'docker exec -it <container_id> /bin/bash' (or /bin/sh for Alpine). The '-it' flag makes the session interactive with a TTY.

questions.title: What is the purpose of the docker exec command?
questions.answer: To run an auxiliary process inside a container that is already running. It is the standard tool for interactive shell debugging or running one-off scripts against a live DB container.

questions.title: How do you stop a running Docker container?
questions.answer: Using 'docker stop <container_id>'. This sends a SIGTERM signal to the process, allowing it to shut down gracefully before being killed.

questions.title: What command is used to list all Docker containers?
questions.answer: 'docker ps' lists running containers. 'docker ps -a' lists all containers, including those that have stopped or exited.

questions.title: How do you see all running containers?
questions.answer: Simply run the command 'docker ps'.

questions.title: What is the purpose of the docker ps command?
questions.answer: To provide a status overview of containers, showing IDs, image names, command used, creation time, status (up/down), ports, and names.

questions.title: How can you remove a stopped container in Docker?
questions.answer: Using 'docker rm <container_id>'. You cannot remove a running container unless you use the '-f' (force) flag.

questions.title: How do you remove a paused container?
questions.answer: You must first unpause it using 'docker unpause', then stop it, and then remove it. Alternatively, 'docker rm -f' will remove it directly.

questions.title: How do you remove stopped containers, unused networks, and dangling images?
questions.answer: Using the 'docker system prune' command. This is the 'cleanup' command for Docker.

questions.title: What are Docker container states?
questions.answer: States include: Created, Restarting, Running, Removing, Paused, Exited, and Dead. You check them via 'docker ps -a' or 'docker inspect'.

questions.title: What happens when a Docker container exits?
questions.answer: The process stops, and resources (CPU/RAM) are released, but the container's file system remains on the host disk until the container is explicitly removed ('docker rm').

questions.title: How do you update an existing Docker container?
questions.answer: You cannot 'update' a running container's image. You must stop the container, remove it, and 'docker run' a new one using the updated image.

questions.title: How would you update a running container without downtime?
questions.answer: This requires an orchestrator like Docker Swarm or Kubernetes. You use a 'Rolling Update' strategy where new containers are started before old ones are stopped, often managed via a load balancer.

questions.title: How do you ensure that Docker containers are stateless?
questions.answer: By never storing important data inside the container's writable layer. All persistent data (DB files, uploads) must be stored in external Volumes or Bind Mounts.

questions.title: Explain Docker volumes and why they are used?
questions.answer: Volumes are specialized directories used to bypass the container's storage layer. They are used for data persistence and sharing data between containers, as they are not deleted when a container stops.

questions.title: How do you manage data in Docker containers?
questions.answer: Data is managed using three main methods: 1. Volumes (managed by Docker). 2. Bind Mounts (linked to host path). 3. Tmpfs (stored in host memory, never written to disk).

questions.title: How can you mount a host directory into a Docker container?
questions.answer: Using the '-v' or '--mount' flag. Example: 'docker run -v /host/path:/container/path image_name'.

questions.title: How can you share data between Docker containers?
questions.answer: By mounting the same Volume to multiple containers simultaneously. Any changes made by one container are instantly visible to the others.

questions.title: What is a Docker volume driver, and how do you use it?
questions.answer: Volume drivers allow you to store data on external storage (like AWS EBS, Azure Disks, or NFS). You use it with the '--driver' flag when creating a volume.

questions.title: How do you handle persistent storage in Docker in a production environment?
questions.answer: In production, managed Volumes with cloud-specific drivers (like CSI drivers) are used to ensure data is backed up, redundant, and can move with the container if it migrates to another host.

questions.title: How do you handle persistent storage in a distributed Docker environment?
questions.answer: Distributed environments use Network File Systems (NFS) or Cloud Storage plugins so that any node in the cluster can access the same persistent data volume.

questions.title: What is a Docker network?
questions.answer: It is an infrastructure that allows containers to communicate with each other and the outside world. Docker creates virtual interfaces and bridges to route this traffic.

questions.title: What is the default network mode for Docker containers?
questions.answer: The default is the 'bridge' network. It assigns a private IP to each container and allows them to communicate with each other on that host.

questions.title: What is the default bridge network in Docker?
questions.answer: It is a software-defined bridge named 'bridge' (usually on the subnet 172.17.0.0/16) created by Docker when it is installed.

questions.title: What is the default IP address of Docker host?
questions.answer: Typically, the Docker bridge 'docker0' takes the IP '172.17.0.1'. This serves as the default gateway for all containers on the default bridge.

questions.title: How do you create a custom Docker network for containers?
questions.answer: Using 'docker network create --driver <type> <name>'. Custom bridge networks allow containers to use 'automatic service discovery' via container names.

questions.title: What is the role of docker network create?
questions.answer: To define a specific communication boundary. Containers on different custom networks cannot talk to each other, providing an extra layer of network security.

questions.title: How do you manage Docker container networking at scale?
questions.answer: At scale, 'overlay' networks are used to bridge traffic between multiple physical hosts, or a CNI (Container Network Interface) is used in Kubernetes to manage complex routing.

questions.title: What is Docker Compose?
questions.answer: It is a tool used for orchestrating multi-container applications, allowing you to define services (DB, Web, Cache) in one YAML file and manage their entire lifecycle together.

questions.title: How does Docker Compose help in managing multi-container applications?
questions.answer: It simplifies management by creating shared networks and volumes automatically, maintaining service dependencies, and allowing for easy environment configuration (environment variables).

questions.title: How do you handle multi-container environments with Docker Compose?
questions.answer: By using the 'docker-compose.yml' file to define services. Running 'docker-compose up' starts all services, and 'docker-compose scale' can increase the number of instances for a service.

questions.title: What is the purpose of docker-compose.yml?
questions.answer: It is the configuration file for Docker Compose. It defines the images, ports, volumes, and networks for every container in a multi-container app.

questions.title: What is the docker-compose.override.yml file?
questions.answer: It is used to store local configuration overrides. When you run 'docker-compose up', it automatically merges this file with the main file, making it perfect for dev-specific settings.

questions.title: How can you use Docker Compose to manage microservices?
questions.answer: By defining each microservice as a 'service' in the YAML file. Compose handles linking them together on a private network, allowing them to communicate using service names as hostnames.

questions.title: What is the Docker Hub?
questions.answer: It is the official, world's largest public registry of Docker images, providing millions of community and official images like Ubuntu, MySQL, and Nginx.

questions.title: What is a Docker registry?
questions.answer: A registry is a storage and distribution system for named Docker images. Images can be 'pushed' to the registry for storage and 'pulled' by others for use.

questions.title: What is the docker pull command used for?
questions.answer: To download an image from a registry (like Docker Hub) to your local machine so you can build containers from it.

questions.title: What is the significance of the docker pull and docker push commands?
questions.answer: They are the 'sync' commands of Docker. 'Push' shares your local image with the team/world via a registry; 'Pull' retrieves updates from others.

questions.title: What is the role of a Docker registry, and how do you manage your private registry?
questions.answer: The role is to centralize image management. Private registries are managed using Docker's official 'registry' image or enterprise tools like Harbor, JFrog Artifactory, or AWS ECR.

questions.title: How do you create a private Docker registry for internal use?
questions.answer: You can run the 'registry:2' container on a server. For security, you must configure TLS/HTTPS and set up basic authentication for users.

questions.title: What is the docker logs command used for?
questions.answer: To fetch the stdout and stderr logs from a container. This is the primary way to debug an application running inside a Docker container.

questions.title: How can you inspect a Docker container?
questions.answer: Using 'docker inspect <container_id>'. It returns a detailed JSON object containing every configuration detail about the container (Network, Mounts, State).

questions.title: What is the role of docker inspect in debugging a container?
questions.answer: It helps identify misconfigurations such as incorrect port mappings, unmounted volumes, wrong environment variables, or unexpected exit codes.

questions.title: How can you monitor the performance of a running Docker container?
questions.answer: Locally, use 'docker stats'. In production, you use tools like Prometheus, Grafana, and cAdvisor to collect and visualize container metrics.

questions.title: How do you monitor the resource usage of Docker containers?
questions.answer: By setting CPU and memory limits in the container configuration and monitoring them using the Docker API or external monitoring agents.

questions.title: How do you monitor Docker containers in production?
questions.answer: Through full-stack monitoring solutions like Datadog, New Relic, or ELK (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) for log aggregation and metric tracking.

questions.title: How do you manage logs in a Dockerized environment?
questions.answer: By using Docker logging drivers (e.g., json-file, syslog, gelf, fluentd) to forward logs from the container to a centralized log management server.

questions.title: How do you manage container logs using Docker?
questions.answer: By default, Docker stores logs in JSON files on the host. For active management, you use 'docker logs' or configure log rotation to prevent disk exhaustion.

questions.title: How would you set up a logging and monitoring solution for production?
questions.answer: Implement an 'EFK' stack (Elasticsearch, Fluentd, Kibana). Fluentd acts as the collector that scrapes logs from all nodes and sends them to Elasticsearch for analysis.

questions.title: How do you handle logs and monitoring for Docker containers in production?
questions.answer: By aggregating logs via the Docker log-driver and visualizing performance with a monitoring agent installed on the Docker host.

questions.title: How do you handle container logs and metrics in a distributed environment?
questions.answer: Using a 'Sidecar' pattern (in K8s) or a global service (in Swarm) that collects logs from all containers on all nodes and pushes them to a central repo.

questions.title: How do you implement a logging solution in Swarm or Kubernetes?
questions.answer: By using DaemonSets (K8s) to ensure a log-collection pod runs on every node, capturing logs from the node's filesystem where Docker writes them.

questions.title: How would you troubleshoot a non-starting Docker container?
questions.answer: 1. Run 'docker ps -a' to see the exit code. 2. Check 'docker logs'. 3. Use 'docker inspect' to check entrypoints. 4. Try running it interactively with 'docker run -it --entrypoint /bin/sh image_name'.

questions.title: What are some strategies to troubleshoot Docker containers at scale?
questions.answer: Centralized logging is key. Additionally, using 'Distributed Tracing' (Jaeger/Zipkin) helps follow a request across multiple container services to find where it fails.

questions.title: What are environment variables in Docker?
questions.answer: They are key-value pairs used to pass dynamic configuration (like DB credentials or API keys) into a container without hardcoding them into the image.

questions.title: How would you expose environment variables to a container?
questions.answer: Using the '-e' flag in 'docker run' or by defining an 'environment' section in a docker-compose.yml file. You can also use an '.env' file.

questions.title: What is Docker Swarm and how does it differ from Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Swarm is Docker's built-in, easy-to-use orchestrator. It is simpler to set up but less flexible than Kubernetes, which has a much larger feature set and ecosystem support.

questions.title: What is the difference between a container and a service in Swarm?
questions.answer: A service is the logical definition of an application (image + replicas). A container (task) is the individual physical instance running on a node to fulfill that service definition.

questions.title: How do you perform rolling updates in Docker Swarm?
questions.answer: By running 'docker service update --image <new_image> <service_name>'. Swarm updates instances one-by-one to ensure zero downtime.

questions.title: Explain the architecture of Docker Swarm and how it compares to Kubernetes.
questions.answer: Swarm uses 'Manager' nodes (raft consensus) and 'Worker' nodes. It uses a declarative model similar to K8s but is more tightly integrated into the Docker CLI.

questions.title: What is a multi-node Docker Swarm cluster?
questions.answer: It is a group of physical or virtual machines running Docker that have been joined together into a cluster. Managers coordinate the distribution of tasks among workers.

questions.title: How do you manage containers using Kubernetes vs Docker Swarm?
questions.answer: In Swarm, you use 'docker service'. In Kubernetes, you use 'kubectl' to manage Pods, Deployments, and Services. K8s is significantly more complex but more robust for large apps.

questions.title: Explain the concept of Docker container orchestration.
questions.answer: It is the system that manages the lifecycle of thousands of containers, handling networking, scale-up/down, health checks, and cross-host communication.

questions.title: What is container orchestration, and why is it important in microservices?
questions.answer: In microservices, you have many moving parts. Orchestration is vital because it automates the 'plumbing' (discovery and load balancing) so services can find and talk to each other.

questions.title: How do you scale a Docker container?
questions.answer: Manually by running more 'docker run' commands, or in an orchestrator by using 'scale' commands (e.g., 'docker service scale myservice=10').

questions.title: How can you scale an application using Docker?
questions.answer: By putting a load balancer (like Nginx or HAProxy) in front of multiple containers running the same image, distributing incoming traffic among them.

questions.title: How would you scale Docker containers in a distributed environment?
questions.answer: By using a cluster manager (K8s/Swarm) to spread containers across multiple physical nodes to increase compute capacity and ensure high availability.

questions.title: How many containers can run on a single host?
questions.answer: There is no fixed limit. It is limited only by the host's resources (CPU, RAM, disk space) and the Linux kernel's process limit (PID limit).

questions.title: How do you set up load balancing for containers across multiple hosts?
questions.answer: Usually via an orchestrator's 'Ingress' network or an external load balancer (like AWS ELB) that routes traffic to the nodes where the containers are running.

questions.title: What is Docker's role in microservices architectures?
questions.answer: Docker provides the 'packaging' for each microservice, ensuring that Service A (Python) doesn't conflict with Service B (Node.js) on the same server.

questions.title: How would you implement service discovery in a Dockerized environment?
questions.answer: Docker custom networks have a built-in DNS server. Containers can find each other using their container_name as the hostname.

questions.title: How do you manage Docker container security in production?
questions.answer: Using security scanning tools (Snyk/Clair), limiting kernel capabilities (--cap-drop), and isolating containers into separate virtual networks.

questions.title: What are the best practices for securing Docker containers and images?
questions.answer: 1. Use minimal images. 2. Don't run as root. 3. Scan for vulnerabilities. 4. Use read-only root filesystems. 5. Limit CPU/RAM to prevent DoS attacks.

questions.title: How do you manage secrets in Docker Swarm or Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Both have a 'Secret' object type. Secrets are encrypted in transit and only mounted as temporary files (tmpfs) in memory for authorized containers.

questions.title: How do you manage secrets, such as API keys, in Docker?
questions.answer: Avoid environment variables for sensitive data as they appear in 'inspect'. Use Docker Secrets (Swarm) or mount secret files into the container.

questions.title: What is a Docker image vulnerability, and how do you scan for them?
questions.answer: A vulnerability is an old/insecure library in the image. You scan them using 'docker scan' (integrated Snyk) or specialized tools like Trivy or Anchore.

questions.title: What is Docker security scanning in a CI/CD pipeline?
questions.answer: It is an automated step where images are checked for known CVEs (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures). If vulnerabilities are found, the build is failed.

questions.title: What is Docker Content Trust?
questions.answer: A feature (DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=1) that allows you to sign images with a digital key. Docker will only pull and run images that have been signed by a trusted publisher.

questions.title: How do you secure Docker daemon?
questions.answer: By protecting the Docker socket (unix:///var/run/docker.sock) and configuring the daemon to only accept connections over TLS/HTTPS with client certificates.

questions.title: What are Docker health checks?
questions.answer: An instruction in a Dockerfile (HEALTHCHECK) that tells Docker how to test if the app inside is still working (e.g., running a curl command against localhost).

questions.title: How would you implement container health checks in production?
questions.answer: By defining health check parameters (interval, timeout, retries) in the docker-compose or service definition so the orchestrator can restart failed instances.

questions.title: How can you use Docker in a CI/CD pipeline?
questions.answer: Containers are used as 'build environments' to ensure identical builds, and the final application is packaged as an image to be deployed automatically.

questions.title: How would you set up a CI/CD pipeline with Docker and Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Git Push -> Jenkins builds image -> Push to Registry -> Helm upgrade -> Kubernetes pulls new image and performs a rolling update.

questions.title: What is the role of Docker Desktop in local development?
questions.answer: It provides a GUI and a bundled VM (for Windows/Mac) to run Docker, including a local single-node Kubernetes cluster for testing.

questions.title: What is Docker Desktop's role in enterprise environments?
questions.answer: It provides standardized dev environments for teams and includes enterprise features like centralized management and security policy enforcement.

questions.title: What are Docker labels?
questions.answer: Metadata in the form of key-value pairs (e.g., version="1.0", maintainer="admin") that help organize images and containers.

questions.title: What is a Docker plugin?
questions.answer: Extensions that add new features to Docker, such as custom volume drivers (storing data on S3) or network drivers (integrating with Cisco/VMware networking).

questions.title: What are Docker container lifecycle hooks?
questions.answer: In orchestration, these are actions triggered by state changes (e.g., 'PostStart' or 'PreStop'), allowing for custom initialization or graceful cleanup.

questions.title: How can you integrate Docker with enterprise tools?
questions.answer: Via the Docker API. Monitoring tools (Dynatrace), security tools (Aqua), and automation tools (Ansible) all use this API to manage containers.

questions.title: How do you configure Docker for high availability?
questions.answer: By running multiple replicas of a service across different nodes in a Swarm/Kubernetes cluster with a load balancer in front.

questions.title: How would you optimize Docker for large-scale production?
questions.answer: Implement layer caching, use a local registry mirror to save bandwidth, and use 'Prometheus' for real-time alerting on resource bottlenecks.

questions.title: How do you ensure application resilience?
questions.answer: By using 'Self-healing' features where the orchestrator automatically detects a dead container and restarts a new one on a healthy node.

questions.title: How do you implement Blue-Green deployments using Docker?
questions.answer: By running two identical environments (Blue and Green). You deploy the new version to Green, test it, and then switch the Load Balancer traffic from Blue to Green.

questions.title: How do you check the version of Docker installed?
questions.answer: Using the 'docker version' command for detailed info, or 'docker --version' for a quick summary.

questions.title: How do you check Docker client and server versions?
questions.answer: Running 'docker version' displays both the Client (CLI) and Server (Engine/Daemon) versions separately.

questions.title: How do you check the Docker status on your system?
questions.answer: On Linux, use 'systemctl status docker'. On Windows/Mac, check the Docker Desktop tray icon or run 'docker info'.

kuberneties-questions.title: Kubernetes Questions
kuberneties-questions.description: A deep-dive technical guide covering K8s Architecture, Workloads, Networking, Storage, Security, and Troubleshooting scenarios.

questions.title: What is Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration platform originally developed by Google. It automates the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications, grouping containers into logical units for easy discovery and management.

questions.title: Why do we need Kubernetes?
questions.answer: As applications move toward microservices, managing hundreds of containers manually becomes impossible. K8s provides self-healing, automated rollouts/rollbacks, horizontal scaling, service discovery, and load balancing, ensuring high availability and efficient resource utilization.

questions.title: Explain Kubernetes Architecture.
questions.answer: Kubernetes follows a leader-worker architecture. It consists of a 'Control Plane' (Master) that manages the cluster state and 'Nodes' (Workers) that run the application containers. The Control Plane makes decisions about the cluster, while Nodes maintain the running pods.

questions.title: What are the main components of Kubernetes Control Plane?
questions.answer: 1. kube-apiserver: The front end and entry point. 2. etcd: The distributed key-value store for cluster data. 3. kube-scheduler: Assigns pods to nodes. 4. kube-controller-manager: Runs controller processes. 5. cloud-controller-manager: Interacts with cloud providers.

questions.title: What are the main components of Kubernetes Worker Node?
questions.answer: 1. kubelet: The agent that ensures containers are running in a Pod. 2. kube-proxy: Manages network rules and traffic forwarding. 3. Container Runtime: The software responsible for running containers (e.g., containerd, CRI-O).

questions.title: What is the purpose of the Kubernetes API server?
questions.answer: The API server is the central hub for the Kubernetes cluster. It exposes the Kubernetes API, validates and processes REST requests, and serves as the only component that communicates directly with the etcd data store to update cluster state.

questions.title: Describe the role of etcd in Kubernetes.
questions.answer: etcd is a consistent and highly-available key-value store used as the cluster's database. It stores the entire configuration and state of the cluster. If etcd is lost, the cluster cannot recover its state, making its backup critical.

questions.title: What is the role of Controller Manager?
questions.answer: It is a daemon that embeds the core control loops (controllers). It watches the shared state of the cluster via the API server and makes changes to move the 'current state' toward the 'desired state' (e.g., bringing up a new pod if one fails).

questions.title: Describe the role of a Proxy (kube-proxy) in Kubernetes.
questions.answer: kube-proxy is a network proxy that runs on each node. It implements the Kubernetes Service concept by maintaining network rules on the host and performing connection forwarding, allowing Pods to communicate internally and externally.

questions.title: What is kubelet and what does it do?
questions.answer: The kubelet is the primary 'node agent'. it takes a set of PodSpecs and ensures that the containers described in those specs are running and healthy. It reports the status of the pod and the node back to the API server.

questions.title: What is the purpose of kubectl?
questions.answer: kubectl is the command-line interface (CLI) for running commands against Kubernetes clusters. It communicates with the API server to create, update, delete, and inspect resources within the cluster environment.

questions.title: What are the most commonly used kubectl commands?
questions.answer: Common commands include: `get` (list resources), `describe` (detailed info), `apply` (create/update), `logs` (view container output), `exec` (run commands inside), `delete` (remove resource), and `top` (monitor usage).

questions.title: Explain the concept of Container Orchestration.
questions.answer: It is the automated management of the container lifecycle. This includes provisioning, deployment, scaling (up/down), networking, load balancing, and health monitoring of containers across a cluster of physical or virtual machines.

questions.title: How does Kubernetes differ from Docker Swarm?
questions.answer: Docker Swarm is simpler and built into Docker but lacks advanced features. K8s is more complex but highly flexible, offering superior auto-scaling, auto-healing, and a vast ecosystem for complex, high-scale production workloads.

questions.title: What is the difference between Docker and Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Docker is a technology used to create, package, and run containers on a single host. Kubernetes is a platform for orchestrating those containers across a cluster. Docker is the 'container', while Kubernetes is the 'captain' of the ship managing the containers.

questions.title: What are pods and what are the commands for managing them?
questions.answer: Pods are the smallest deployable units in K8s, representing a single instance of a running process. Management commands: `kubectl get pods`, `kubectl describe pod <name>`, `kubectl logs <name>`, and `kubectl delete pod <name>`.

questions.title: What is the difference between a Pod and a container?
questions.answer: A container is a single execution environment (like a Docker container). A Pod is a wrapper that can hold one or more containers that share the same network namespace and storage volumes, essentially acting as a 'logical host'.

questions.title: How do you create a Pod?
questions.answer: A pod can be created imperatively using `kubectl run <podname> --image=<image>` or declaratively using a YAML file and the command `kubectl apply -f pod-definition.yaml`.

questions.title: How do you get logs from a Pod?
questions.answer: Using `kubectl logs <pod-name>`. For a multi-container pod, specify the container with `-c <container-name>`. Adding the `-f` flag allows for real-time log streaming (following).

questions.title: How do you execute commands inside a Pod?
questions.answer: Using `kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- <command>`. For an interactive shell, use `kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- /bin/bash` or `/bin/sh` depending on the image.

questions.title: How do you copy files to/from a Pod?
questions.answer: Using the `kubectl cp` command. Syntax: `kubectl cp <local-file> <namespace>/<pod-name>:<remote-path>` to upload, and reversing the arguments to download to your local machine.

questions.title: How do you debug Kubernetes Pods?
questions.answer: Debugging involves checking the status with `get pods`, inspecting events/errors with `describe pod`, analyzing logs with `logs`, and using `exec` to enter the container and check local environment variables or files.

questions.title: Difference between describe pod and inspect pod.
questions.answer: `kubectl describe pod` provides a high-level summary and recent 'Events'. K8s doesn't have an 'inspect' command like Docker; to see raw JSON/YAML data, use `kubectl get pod <name> -o json` or `yaml`.

questions.title: What are init containers, and how are they different from regular containers within a pod?
questions.answer: Init containers run to completion before app containers start. They are used for setup logic (like waiting for a database). Unlike regular containers, if an init container fails, K8s restarts the pod until it succeeds.

questions.title: What is a Sidecar Container?
questions.answer: A sidecar is a secondary container that runs alongside the main container in the same Pod. It provides helper tasks like log shipping, proxying (Envoy in Istio), or monitoring without the main app knowing it exists.

questions.title: What are Native Sidecars (SidecarContainers), and what problem do they solve?
questions.answer: Native sidecars (K8s 1.29+) allow containers in a pod to be marked as sidecars so they start before others and stop last. This solves the issue where sidecars would keep Jobs running even after the main task finished.

questions.title: How does Kubernetes handle Pod disruptions and high availability?
questions.answer: K8s uses Pod Disruption Budgets (PDB) to ensure a minimum number of pods remain available during maintenance. High availability is achieved through Replicas in Deployments, spreading pods across different Nodes or Availability Zones.

questions.title: Name typical Pod error causes and how they can be fixed.
questions.answer: 1. ImagePullBackOff (check secret/name). 2. CrashLoopBackOff (check logs/env). 3. Pending (check resources/taints). 4. OOMKilled (increase memory limit). 5. CreateContainerConfigError (check ConfigMaps/Secrets).

questions.title: What is a multi-container Pod?
questions.answer: It is a single Pod containing two or more containers that share resources like network (localhost) and storage volumes. They are tightly coupled and should always be scheduled on the same node together.

questions.title: Can you run multiple containers in a single Pod?
questions.answer: Yes. This is used for patterns like Sidecar, Adapter, and Ambassador. All containers in the Pod share the same IP, port space, and storage, allowing them to communicate efficiently via IPC or localhost.

questions.title: Explain Deployments and the different deployment strategies.
questions.answer: A Deployment provides declarative updates for Pods. Strategies: 1. RollingUpdate (incremental replacement, zero downtime). 2. Recreate (kill all, then start all, involves downtime). 3. Canary or Blue-Green (manually controlled).

questions.title: What is the relationship between a Deployment, ReplicaSet, and Pod?
questions.answer: A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet, and a ReplicaSet manages Pods. When you update a Deployment, it creates a new ReplicaSet and gradually moves pods from the old ReplicaSet to the new one.

questions.title: Difference between Replication Controller and ReplicaSet.
questions.answer: Replication Controller is the older method. ReplicaSet is the successor that supports 'set-based' label selectors (e.g., matching multiple labels simultaneously), whereas Replication Controllers only support equality-based selectors.

questions.title: Explain the difference between a StatefulSet and a Deployment.
questions.answer: Deployments are for stateless apps where pods are interchangeable. StatefulSets are for applications requiring stable network IDs, stable persistent storage (using VolumeClaimTemplates), and ordered deployment/scaling (e.g., Databases).

questions.title: When would you use StatefulSet vs Deployment?
questions.answer: Use Deployment for web servers, APIs, and microservices. Use StatefulSet for databases (MySQL, MongoDB), distributed systems (Zookeeper, Kafka), or any app where the pod needs a fixed identity like 'pod-0'.

questions.title: How does StatefulSet handle Pod identity and ordering?
questions.answer: StatefulSet pods have an ordinal index (0 to N-1). They are created in order (0, then 1...) and deleted in reverse order. Each pod gets a stable hostname (name-0.service) that persists across restarts.

questions.title: What are Headless Services and when would you use them?
questions.answer: A Headless Service (ClusterIP: None) does not have a single IP. Instead, it returns the direct IPs of all backing Pods. It's used with StatefulSets so clients can talk to specific pods (like the Master in a DB cluster).

questions.title: What is the difference between a Deployment, a StatefulSet, and a DaemonSet?
questions.answer: Deployment: General stateless apps. StatefulSet: Persistent/Ordered apps. DaemonSet: Ensures that exactly one copy of a Pod runs on every (or selected) node in the cluster (e.g., logging agents).

questions.title: Explain the differences between a DaemonSet and a ReplicaSet.
questions.answer: A ReplicaSet ensures a total number of pods are running across the cluster. A DaemonSet ensures one pod runs per node. When nodes are added/removed, the DaemonSet automatically adds/removes pods on those nodes.

questions.title: When would you use a DaemonSet?
questions.answer: Use DaemonSets for node-level infrastructure: 1. Log collection daemons (Fluentd, Logstash). 2. Monitoring agents (Prometheus Node Exporter). 3. Storage proxies or network plugins that must exist on every node.

questions.title: How do rolling updates work in a Deployment?
questions.answer: K8s creates a new ReplicaSet and scales it up while scaling down the old ReplicaSet. It uses `maxUnavailable` (max pods down during update) and `maxSurge` (max extra pods created) to ensure zero downtime.

questions.title: What are the different deployment strategies in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: 1. RollingUpdate (Default). 2. Recreate (Downtime). 3. Blue-Green (Separate environments). 4. Canary (Traffic splitting). 5. Shadow (Mirroring traffic).

questions.title: What is Blue-Green deployment?
questions.answer: A strategy where you maintain two identical production environments. One (Blue) is live, the other (Green) is where you deploy the new version. Once tested, you switch traffic at the Service/Load Balancer level from Blue to Green.

questions.title: What is Canary deployment?
questions.answer: A strategy where a new version is deployed to a small subset of users (the 'canaries'). You monitor its health; if successful, you roll it out to the entire cluster. If it fails, you only affect a tiny fraction of users.

questions.title: How do you perform rollbacks in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Using `kubectl rollout undo deployment <name>`. You can also specify a specific revision by adding `--to-revision=N`. Use `kubectl rollout history` to view the available versions.

questions.title: How do you implement zero-downtime Deployments in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: By using `RollingUpdate` combined with `Readiness Probes`. The Readiness probe ensures the new pod is actually ready to handle requests before the old pod is terminated, maintaining continuous service availability.

questions.title: What is a Recreate deployment strategy?
questions.answer: It terminates all existing pods before starting new ones. It is used when an application cannot run multiple versions simultaneously (e.g., due to schema changes) but involves noticeable downtime.

questions.title: What are Kubernetes Services and the different types?
questions.answer: Services provide a stable IP/DNS to a set of Pods. Types: 1. ClusterIP (internal). 2. NodePort (external on node port). 3. LoadBalancer (Cloud external). 4. ExternalName (CNAME record).

questions.title: What is ClusterIP Service?
questions.answer: The default service type. It provides a stable IP address accessible only from within the cluster. It load-balances internal traffic among the pods identified by the selector.

questions.title: What is NodePort Service?
questions.answer: Exposes the service on a static port (30000-32767) on each Node’s IP. You can access the service from outside the cluster using `<NodeIP>:<NodePort>`.

questions.title: What is LoadBalancer Service?
questions.answer: Typically used in cloud environments (AWS, GCP, Azure). It creates a cloud provider's load balancer and automatically assigns an external IP that routes to the service's ClusterIP/NodePort.

questions.title: What is ExternalName Service?
questions.answer: A service that maps to a DNS name (CNAME record) instead of using selectors. It is used to alias external services (like an RDS database) so they can be accessed via a local K8s service name.

questions.title: How does Service Discovery work in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: K8s uses Environment Variables and DNS. Every service gets a DNS record (service.namespace.svc.cluster.local). Pods use the cluster DNS (CoreDNS) to look up these service names to resolve IPs.

questions.title: How does DNS work in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: A cluster-wide DNS service (CoreDNS) is automatically configured. When services are created, the API server notifies CoreDNS to create A/SRV records. Pods inherit DNS settings to resolve these records.

questions.title: How does Kubernetes enforce communication boundaries between Pods?
questions.answer: By default, K8s allows all-to-all communication. Boundaries are enforced using 'Network Policies' (pod firewalls) that define ingress and egress rules based on labels and namespaces.

questions.title: How can you achieve communication between Pods on different Nodes?
questions.answer: This is handled by the Container Network Interface (CNI) plugin (like Calico or Flannel). It creates an 'Overlay Network' ensuring every Pod has a unique IP across the entire cluster cluster-wide.

questions.title: Explain the concept of Ingress in Kubernetes.
questions.answer: Ingress is an API object that manages external HTTP/S access to services. It provides URL-based routing (e.g., domain.com/api), SSL termination, and name-based virtual hosting.

questions.title: What is an Ingress Controller?
questions.answer: Ingress is just a set of rules. The Ingress Controller is the actual application (Reverse Proxy) that implements those rules, such as Nginx, HAProxy, Traefik, or Istio Ingress Gateway.

questions.title: What is the Kubernetes Gateway API, and how is it different from Ingress?
questions.answer: Gateway API is the modern successor to Ingress. It is more modular, supports TCP/UDP (not just HTTP), and splits configuration into separate roles (GatewayClass, Gateway, and Routes) for better multi-tenancy.

questions.title: What is a Network Policy in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: A Network Policy is a specification of how groups of pods are allowed to communicate with each other and other network endpoints. It works at the L3/L4 level, essentially acting as a pod-level firewall.

questions.title: What is CoreDNS? How do you configure and use it?
questions.answer: CoreDNS is a modular DNS server that acts as the cluster DNS. It is configured via a ConfigMap (Corefile). It is used automatically by Pods to resolve service names into IPs.

questions.title: What is EndpointSlice?
questions.answer: EndpointSlice is a scalable version of Endpoints. It groups network endpoints together to reduce the performance overhead of updating large services with thousands of pods.

questions.title: How does kube-proxy handle service traffic?
questions.answer: Kube-proxy typically uses 'IPtables' or 'IPVS' modes to create rules on each node. When traffic hits a Service IP, these rules redirect the packets to one of the healthy backend Pod IPs.

questions.title: What is a Namespace?
questions.answer: A Namespace is a logical partition in a Kubernetes cluster used to isolate resources. It allows for multi-tenancy, helping different teams or environments (Dev/Prod) use the same cluster without interference.

questions.title: Why do we use Namespaces in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Namespaces prevent naming collisions, allow for granular access control (RBAC), and enable resource limits/quotas per team, ensuring one group doesn't consume all cluster resources.

questions.title: How would you isolate resources for multiple teams and avoid naming conflicts?
questions.answer: Create a unique Namespace for each team. Apply Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) to limit team access to their namespace and use ResourceQuotas to cap their consumption.

questions.title: What do you understand by ResourceQuota?
questions.answer: A ResourceQuota object provides constraints that limit aggregate resource consumption per namespace. It can cap the total CPU, Memory, or the number of objects (like Pods or Services) allowed in that namespace.

questions.title: What do you understand by LimitRange?
questions.answer: A LimitRange is a policy to constrain the resource allocations (Limits/Requests) for individual containers or pods within a namespace, ensuring they aren't too small or too large.

questions.title: How does Kubernetes handle resource limits and requests?
questions.answer: Requests are used for scheduling (finding a node with enough space). Limits are enforced at runtime by the container runtime and OS kernel to ensure a container doesn't exceed its allocation.

questions.title: What's the difference between resource requests and limits?
questions.answer: Request: The minimum resource guaranteed to a container (Scheduler uses this). Limit: The maximum resource a container is allowed to consume (Cgroups enforce this).

questions.title: What is QoS (Quality of Service) in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: QoS is a mechanism K8s uses to decide which pods to evict first when a node runs out of resources. It is determined automatically based on the pod's requests and limits configuration.

questions.title: What are the different QoS classes in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: 1. Guaranteed (Request == Limit). 2. Burstable (Request < Limit). 3. BestEffort (No requests/limits). Guaranteed pods are the last to be evicted.

questions.title: What happens if a Pod exceeds memory/CPU limits?
questions.answer: If a pod exceeds its **Memory** limit, it is OOM (Out Of Memory) killed by the kernel. If it exceeds its **CPU** limit, it is 'throttled' (slowed down) but usually not killed.

questions.title: What happens if a Pod resource needs to grow beyond the assigned limits?
questions.answer: It cannot. Kubernetes uses kernel cgroups to enforce limits. If the pod attempts to use more, it will be throttled (CPU) or killed (Memory). To grow, the YAML must be updated and the pod restarted.

questions.title: How do you manage Kubernetes resource quotas in multi-tenant environments?
questions.answer: By applying a ResourceQuota YAML to each tenant's Namespace. This ensures one tenant's load spikes don't starve other tenants of CPU, RAM, or storage.

questions.title: How do you implement Kubernetes cluster multi-tenancy?
questions.answer: Using: 1. Namespaces. 2. RBAC. 3. Network Policies (isolation). 4. ResourceQuotas. 5. Taints/Tolerations or Node Affinity to keep tenant workloads on specific hardware.

questions.title: What do you understand by ConfigMap?
questions.answer: A ConfigMap is an API object used to store non-confidential data in key-value pairs. It allows you to decouple environment-specific configurations from container images, making apps portable.

questions.title: How do you create a ConfigMap?
questions.answer: Imperatively: `kubectl create configmap <name> --from-literal=key=value` or from a file. Declaratively: Defining a YAML of kind `ConfigMap` and using `kubectl apply`.

questions.title: How do you mount ConfigMaps as volumes?
questions.answer: In the PodSpec, define a volume of type `configMap`. Then, in the container spec, use `volumeMounts` to mount that volume to a specific file path inside the container.

questions.title: How do you inject ConfigMaps as environment variables?
questions.answer: Use the `envFrom` field in the container spec to inject all keys, or the `env` field with `valueFrom` to inject specific keys from the ConfigMap as environment variables.

questions.title: What are ConfigMaps and Secrets in Kubernetes, and how do they differ?
questions.answer: ConfigMaps are for plain-text configuration. Secrets are for sensitive data (passwords, tokens). Secrets are Base64 encoded by default and can be encrypted at rest in etcd.

questions.title: What are Secrets in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Secrets are objects used to store and manage sensitive information safely. K8s avoids plain-text exposure in the YAML and provides better protection than hardcoding secrets in images.

questions.title: How do you create a Secret?
questions.answer: Using `kubectl create secret generic <name> --from-literal=key=secretvalue`. Like ConfigMaps, they can also be created from files or declarative YAML manifests.

questions.title: What are the different types of Secrets in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: 1. `Opaque` (generic). 2. `kubernetes.io/service-account-token`. 3. `kubernetes.io/dockercfg`. 4. `kubernetes.io/tls` (for certificates).

questions.title: How do you encrypt Kubernetes secrets in etcd?
questions.answer: By configuring an `EncryptionConfiguration` resource on the API server. This uses a provider (like AES-GCM or a KMS) to encrypt Secret data before it is written to the etcd disk.

questions.title: What are best practices for managing Secrets in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: 1. Enable Encryption at Rest. 2. Use RBAC to limit access. 3. Integrate with external vaults (HashiCorp Vault). 4. Avoid checking Secrets into Git (use tools like SealedSecrets).

questions.title: How do you use Secrets in Pods?
questions.answer: Secrets can be injected as Environment Variables or mounted as Files in a volume. When mounted as a volume, the secret value is projected into the file system in memory (tmpfs).

questions.title: What are volumes in Kubernetes (EmptyDir, HostPath, PV, PVC)?
questions.answer: Volumes provide persistent or ephemeral storage. `EmptyDir` is scratch space; `HostPath` uses node disk; `PV` is cluster-wide storage; `PVC` is a request for that storage.

questions.title: What is EmptyDir volume?
questions.answer: An ephemeral volume created when a Pod is assigned to a Node. It is empty initially and is deleted permanently when the Pod is removed from that node.

questions.title: What is HostPath volume?
questions.answer: It mounts a file or directory from the host node's filesystem into your Pod. It's used for system-level pods (like log collectors) but is generally avoided for normal apps for security reasons.

questions.title: What are Persistent Volumes (PVs) and PersistentVolumeClaims (PVCs)?
questions.answer: PV is a piece of storage in the cluster (the 'disk'). PVC is a request for storage by a user (the 'ticket'). PVCs bind to PVs that meet their size and access mode requirements.

questions.title: What is the difference between PV and PVC?
questions.answer: PV is a resource in the cluster managed by admins. PVC is a request for that resource by a developer. PV represents the actual capacity, while PVC is the logic that claims it.

questions.title: What is a StorageClass?
questions.answer: StorageClass allows admins to describe the 'classes' of storage they offer (e.g., 'fast' SSD vs 'slow' HDD). It enables dynamic provisioning so PVs are created automatically when a PVC is made.

questions.title: What is dynamic volume provisioning?
questions.answer: It allows storage volumes to be created on-demand. When a user creates a PVC, the StorageClass triggers the cloud provider to create the disk and the K8s PV automatically.

questions.title: How does Kubernetes manage storage orchestration?
questions.answer: K8s uses the Container Storage Interface (CSI). Storage vendors write CSI drivers that K8s calls to create, attach, and mount disks to nodes and containers seamlessly.

questions.title: What are the different access modes for Persistent Volumes?
questions.answer: 1. ReadWriteOnce (RWO): One node can mount it. 2. ReadOnlyMany (ROX): Many nodes can mount read-only. 3. ReadWriteMany (RWX): Many nodes can mount read-write.

questions.title: What happens when you delete a PVC?
questions.answer: The behavior depends on the PV's Reclaim Policy: `Retain` (manual cleanup needed), `Delete` (disk deleted immediately), or `Recycle` (scrub files and reuse).

questions.title: How does the Kubernetes Scheduler assign Pods to Nodes?
questions.answer: It uses a 2-step process: 1. Filtering (finding nodes that meet pod requirements). 2. Scoring (ranking filtered nodes to find the best fit based on resource availability).

questions.title: What factors does the Kubernetes Scheduler consider?
questions.answer: Resource requirements, Taints/Tolerations, Node Affinity, Data locality, Inter-pod affinity/anti-affinity, and dead-lines.

questions.title: What is Taint and Toleration?
questions.answer: Taints are applied to Nodes to repel certain Pods. Tolerations are applied to Pods to allow them to stay on tained Nodes. They work together to ensure pods don't run on inappropriate nodes.

questions.title: Explain the concept of Taints and Tolerations.
questions.answer: Taints 'mark' a node (e.g., 'this node is for GPU work'). Only Pods with a matching Toleration can be scheduled there. It’s like a 'Keep Out' sign that only certain pods can ignore.

questions.title: How do Taints and Tolerations work together?
questions.answer: Taints are on Nodes; Tolerations are on Pods. A pod will only schedule on a tainted node if it 'tolerates' that specific taint. If a node has no taints, any pod can schedule there.

questions.title: What is Node Affinity?
questions.answer: Node Affinity is a set of rules used by the scheduler to 'attract' Pods to specific nodes based on labels. It is a more flexible version of the `nodeSelector`.

questions.title: What are Affinity and Anti-Affinity?
questions.answer: Affinity pushes pods toward specific nodes or pods. Anti-Affinity pushes pods away from them (e.g., to ensure two copies of a pod aren't on the same node for HA).

questions.title: What is Pod Affinity?
questions.answer: Pod Affinity ensures that certain pods are scheduled on the same node (or in the same zone) because they communicate heavily and need low latency.

questions.title: What is Pod Anti-Affinity?
questions.answer: Pod Anti-Affinity ensures pods are NOT scheduled on the same node. This is critical for high availability, ensuring that if one node fails, the entire service doesn't go down.

questions.title: What is the difference between Node Affinity and Taints/Tolerations?
questions.answer: Node Affinity 'attracts' pods to nodes. Taints/Tolerations allow nodes to 'repel' pods. Affinity is pod-centric (where should I go?); Taints are node-centric (who can come here?).

questions.title: What is Node Selector?
questions.answer: The simplest form of node selection constraint. You specify a label in the PodSpec, and the pod will only run on nodes that have that exact key-value label pair.

questions.title: How do you manage labels in Kubernetes commands?
questions.answer: Using `kubectl label pods <name> key=value`. You can also filter using labels: `kubectl get pods -l key=value` or delete using them: `kubectl delete pods -l key=value`.

questions.title: Explain the use of Labels and Selectors in Kubernetes.
questions.answer: Labels are metadata attached to objects. Selectors are used to query and filter those objects. For example, a Service uses a Selector to find which Pods it should route traffic to.

questions.title: What are Labels in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Labels are key-value pairs attached to objects (like Pods). They are used to organize and select subsets of objects but do not have direct functional impact on the container runtime.

questions.title: What are Selectors in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: Selectors are the primary grouping mechanism in K8s. They allow you to identify a set of objects based on their labels (e.g., 'find all pods where app=frontend and env=prod').

questions.title: What is the difference between Labels and Annotations?
questions.answer: Labels are used for identifying and selecting objects. Annotations are for non-identifying metadata (like build IDs or contact info) that tools and libraries can read.

questions.title: How does Kubernetes handle container scaling?
questions.answer: K8s scales containers by adjusting the 'replica' count in a Deployment/ReplicaSet. This can be done manually via `kubectl scale` or automatically using the HPA.

questions.title: What is Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)?
questions.answer: HPA automatically scales the number of pods in a deployment based on observed CPU utilization or other custom metrics to handle traffic spikes.

questions.title: Describe how a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) works.
questions.answer: HPA queries the Metrics Server periodically. It calculates the ratio of 'current metric' vs 'target metric'. If current usage is higher than target, it tells the Deployment to increase replicas.

questions.title: What is Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA)?
questions.answer: VPA automatically sets the resource 'Requests' and 'Limits' for your containers, giving more CPU/RAM to pods that need it and taking it away from those that don't.

questions.title: What is Cluster Autoscaler?
questions.answer: Cluster Autoscaler adds or removes physical/virtual Nodes from the cluster itself when pods cannot be scheduled due to lack of resources or when nodes are underutilized.

questions.title: What is the difference between HPA and VPA?
questions.answer: HPA scales 'out' by adding more pods. VPA scales 'up' by giving existing pods more power (RAM/CPU). Usually, you shouldn't use both on the same metric for the same pod.

questions.title: How does HPA determine when to scale?
questions.answer: By evaluating the equation: `DesiredReplicas = ceil[CurrentReplicas * (CurrentMetric / TargetMetric)]`. If the result differs from the current replica count, K8s adjusts the deployment.

questions.title: What are Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes in Kubernetes?
questions.answer: These are health checks. Liveness: Checks if container is alive (restarts if fail). Readiness: Checks if container is ready for traffic. Startup: Checks if app has finished starting up.

questions.title: What is a Liveness Probe?
questions.answer: A check to see if the container process is still functioning. If a Liveness probe fails, K8s kills the container and starts a new one based on the restart policy.

questions.title: What is a Readiness Probe?
